description:
We are a team of Computer Science students from An-Najah National University, Palestine, passionate about Artificial Intelligence, software development, space technology, and solving real-world challenges through innovation.

Our project, EarthPulse, aims to transform NASA's Earth observation data into meaningful, interactive insights using AI, advanced data visualization, and modern web technologies.
summary: Earth has powerful stories to tell, but much of its scientific data remains difficult to interpret, explore, and access. EarthPulse bridges this gap by transforming real NASA Earth data into an interactive experience that allows people to see, hear, and understand environmental phenomena. Through an interactive Earth map, users explore dust, precipitation,  and wind across available locations and dates. Unlike conventional visualizations, EarthPulse uses scientifically grounded sonification, translating actual measurements into meaningful changes in sound rather than arbitrary background music. Its integrated discovery, pattern-matching, and comparison tools help users investigate environmental changes and similarities. Guided Voice and Pure Sonification provide different ways to engage with the data. Designed for students, educators, researchers, and people with visual impairments, EarthPulse supports a more inclusive and engaging approach to Earth science. By bringing NASA data to life, EarthPulse makes our planet's patterns understandable through both sight and sound.
details:
EarthPulse — Project Details

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

1. How EarthPulse Works

We built EarthPulse to make NASA Earth data easier to explore and understand by combining interactive maps with sound.

Users can choose an environmental phenomenon, such as dust, rain, temperature, or wind, and

explore its data on a map. They can select a location and an available date to see the

measurements and hear how the values are represented through sound.

The main idea is that the sounds are connected to real data, not just background music. For example, changes in rainfall can affect the rhythm, temperature can change the pitch, wind can influence the movement and rhythm of the sound, and dust can affect its texture.

This gives users another way to notice differences between places and understand how environmental conditions change.

2. Main Features

Interactive Earth Map and Sound Studio

The map is where users explore different environmental phenomena, while Sound Studio lets them listen to the data and interact with its sounds.

Users can select locations, explore supported dates, and hear how different measurements affect the audio.

Earth Signal Hunter

We added Earth Signal Hunter to help users find interesting changes in environmental data

without having to search through all the measurements themselves.

It helps identify high values, noticeable changes, and other interesting conditions, then connects the results to their locations on the map.

Earth Echo Finder

Earth Echo Finder helps users discover different places that show similar environmental patterns.

Instead of comparing sounds alone, it compares the actual scientific data and allows users to explore and listen to the results.

Comparison

With Comparison, users can compare two locations or different time periods.

They can see the differences in the measurements and listen to how those differences are

represented through sound.

Guided Voice and Pure Sonification

We included two listening modes to give users different ways to experience the platform.

Guided Voice provides spoken explanations and helps users navigate the experience.

Pure Sonification lets users focus on the sounds generated from the data without spoken explanations.

Scientific Orchestra — In Development

We're also working on Scientific Orchestra as part of Sound Studio.

The goal is to let users combine sounds from multiple environmental phenomena and control each one separately, including its volume and whether it is active.

3. Technologies and Tools

We developed EarthPulse as a web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

We use the Web Audio API to generate and control sounds based on scientific values, while

browser speech synthesis supports the Guided Voice feature.

NASA data is prepared and organized into JSON files that include measurements, geographical

information, dates, and other relevant details.

We also use Node.js for development scripts and testing. The platform includes responsive

layouts, Arabic and English interfaces, and keyboard-based interaction to make it easier for different users to explore.

4. How We Use NASA Data

NASA data is the foundation of EarthPulse.

We use NASA-sourced environmental data, including GEOS-FP atmospheric model output, to explore environmental conditions across supported locations and dates.

We process the available data into structured JSON files so our application can use it for the map, comparisons, and sound generation.

Each sound is connected to a numerical value through a defined mapping. This means the sounds represent changes in scientific data rather than actual recordings of environmental phenomena.

We also take into account the limits of the available data, including supported locations, dates, and missing measurements. Since GEOS-FP provides model-based estimates, we don't present these values as direct satellite measurements or real-time observations.

5. Project Goals and Impact

Our goal with EarthPulse is to make Earth science easier to understand and more interesting to explore.

We want students and teachers to have a different way to learn about environmental phenomena, while also giving researchers and other users tools to explore patterns and compare data.

Accessibility is also an important part of our idea. By combining sound with visual information

and spoken guidance, we hope to make environmental data more accessible to people with visual impairments.

We believe that scientific data shouldn't be limited to numbers, graphs, and maps. It should also be something people can interact with and experience in different ways.

6. Development Status and What's Next

We've developed working versions of the interactive map, data-based audio experience, Earth Signal Hunter, Earth Echo Finder, Comparison, Guided Voice, and Pure Sonification.

We're currently working on integrating and testing these features together to make sure the complete experience works as expected.

Scientific Orchestra is still under development, especially the controls for combining multiple sounds and keeping the data synchronized.

Our next steps are to improve the overall user experience, test accessibility, and expand the environmental data we can support.

With EarthPulse, we're trying to show that NASA Earth data can be explored in a different way, where users don't just look at environmental changes but can also hear and better understand

them.
